caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

The Krausz et al. (2023) analysis code, read (not run) for the meaning of the nom_rwd columns, which DA/Modules/hexLevelAnalyses.py divides by 100 and calls pRwd.

attempts.entry_title: Continuous temporal difference learning and dopamine (Garud & Morris 2026)
attempts.summary: In this dandiset's mouse photometry the behavioural findings held: anticipatory licking was higher in short-ITI sessions and rose with training. The tonic dopamine dip late in long inter-trial intervals held only against a baseline of zero ΔF/F, which the session-wide 405 nm correction forces, and there was no dip against the pre-cue level. The short-ITI reward response did not persist to the next cue as reported. The dip deepened with training, but no reading of methods the paper leaves open matched its r and p together. On the rat maze data held elsewhere, the dopamine ramps and the Gaussian continuous-time TD model fit reproduced, while the recovered value function held only in part.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Garud and Morris (2026) on the dopamine photometry of dandiset 001552 (Floeder et al. 2025), its Figure 4 on tonic dopamine and licking in short-ITI and long-ITI Pavlovian sessions, and on the Krausz et al. (2023) hex-level table from Mendeley Data, its Figures 2, 3 and 5 on dopamine ramps, velocity and model comparison in freely moving rats.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Garud & Morris (2026) from dandiset 001552 and the Krausz hex-level table

outcomes.statement: The Floeder dataset holds 18 mice, each with 16 to 24 sessions, alternating between short-ITI and long-ITI conditions across days.
outcomes.source: Methods, Datasets, paragraph 2; Methods, Floeder (2025) dataset, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Mice (n = 18) completed 16–24 sessions each, alternating between short-ITI (~15 s median inter-trial interval) and long-ITI (~45 s) conditions across days
outcomes.notes: 18 mice (9 JF-FP, 9 JF-dLight-ramp2) have photometry and event logs, with 16 to 24 sessions each (16 to 24 also before two duplicate files are counted once), and every mouse has short-ITI and long-ITI sessions. Session medians of the inter-cue interval are 14.2 to 16.9 s (median 16.6) in the short class and 37.0 to 72.8 s (median 53.7) in the long class, so the short value fits the Methods' ~15 s and the long value the Results' ~55 s. The sessions are in blocks (8 long then 8 short; or 7 or 8 long, 8 short, 7 or 8 long), not alternating day by day as the statement says; the criterion does not test the order. The dandiset also holds 9 JF-VR-FP mice with photometry only, which the criterion's count leaves out.
deviations: Two files that hold the same recording as another day's file (JF-dLight-ramp2-F2 Day4, JF-dLight-ramp2-F4 Day6) are counted once, at the first day.

outcomes.statement: Mice show higher anticipatory lick rates in short-ITI sessions than in long-ITI sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on tonic dopamine (Fig. 4A); Figure 4A legend
outcomes.quote: Mice in short-ITI sessions showed higher anticipatory lick rates (Fig. 4A)
outcomes.notes: Lick rate 5 to 8 s after cue onset, short 2.393 Hz against long 1.600 Hz per mouse, paired t(17) = 4.15, p = 0.00067, higher in 16 of 18 mice; the two readings of the per-mouse rate give the same values to three decimals (p 0.00067 and 0.00068). Lick onsets are event code 5, the only lick-onset code in the files.

outcomes.statement: During the late inter-trial interval of long-ITI sessions, dopamine settles below baseline, while in short-ITI sessions a slowly decaying reward response does not resolve before the next trial.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on tonic dopamine (Fig. 4B); Figure 4B legend; Discussion, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: long-ITI dopamine settled reliably below baseline ... while the short-ITI trace showed a slowly decaying reward response that did not resolve before the next trial (Fig. 4B)
outcomes.notes: Long-ITI part holds under all eight readings (correction x ITI reference x observation rule) - the per-mouse late-ITI ΔF/F is below zero in 18 of 18 mice, mean -0.0036 to -0.0061, t(17) -11.6 to -13.7, one-tailed p 6.5e-11 to 8.2e-10, over 212 long-ITI sessions. The short-ITI part does not hold - the last kept bin before the next cue is below zero, mean -0.0067 (SEM 0.0011) under the trial reading and -0.0056 (SEM 0.0007) under the sample reading, above zero in 1 and 0 of 18 mice. On the criterion's baseline of ΔF/F zero the short-ITI reward response has resolved, and gone below zero, before the next trial. Of the ITI references the paper best supports the one from reward (median reward to next cue 7.57 s short and 44.72 s long, the Results' ~8 s and the Methods' ~45 s; cue to cue the long median is 53.7 s), which is adopted where one reading is needed; the outcome is the same under all eight. Both corrections regress the 405 nm signal over the whole session, so each session's mean ΔF/F is zero by construction (fit reading median 2e-08, largest 0.003 in absolute value; own reading largest 4e-18), and stretches without transients come out below zero; a late-ITI value below the criterion's baseline of zero is partly set by this centering, and the test cannot separate a tonic dip from it. Against a pre-cue baseline, outside the criterion, there is no dip - the late-ITI level minus the level 5 to 0 s before the cue is 0.0003 (t(17) = 1.03, p = 0.32, lower in 8 of 18 mice; fit, reward, trials). Against the long-ITI late-ITI level, the short-ITI last bin is not higher (-0.0067 against -0.0046, paired t(17) = -1.87, p = 0.078, higher in 5 of 18), so the short-ITI part fails under that comparison too. Both readings of the criterion's baseline are asked of a reader in questions/garud-2026.yaml. A cue-locked trace confirms the short-ITI alignment - ΔF/F rises in the first second after the cue in 143 of 144 short-ITI sessions.
deviations: The paper reports no test for this panel; the one-sample one-tailed t-test across mice is the criterion's, taken from the paper's test of the stationary dip.
The session's tonic value is the mean over trials of each trial's mean over its kept bins in the window, a standard choice the Methods do not state.
Photometry samples are placed on the event clock by a fit of TTL2 rising edges to cue times; the files state no link between the two clocks.
The files hold no depositor ΔF/F (processing/ holds only the task parameters), so ΔF/F is formed from the raw 470 and 405 nm channels under the criterion's two readings.

outcomes.statement: In long-ITI sessions the tonic dopamine dip deepens across training sessions (r = -0.29, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on tonic dopamine (Fig. 4D); Figure 4D-E legend
outcomes.quote: we found that the dip deepened across training sessions as V̂ was learned (Fig. 4D, r=-0.29, p<1e-3)

statistics.test: linear mixed-effects model with random intercepts and slopes per subject

outcomes.notes: Over 16 readings (8 tonic readings x 2 session numberings) the fixed slope on session number is negative in 16, below p = 0.05 in 10 and below p = 0.001 in 2. Under the first-listed tonic and session readings (fit, reward, trials, all sessions) the slope is -8.3e-05 ΔF/F per session, p = 0.0043; Pearson r is -0.128 pooled (reading a, out of tolerance) and -0.283 after removing each mouse's mean (reading b, within tolerance), the value given as measured. The two readings with p below 0.001 (fit and own, cue, samples, all sessions, p = 0.00064 and 0.00060) have r -0.13 pooled and -0.35 within mice, both out of tolerance. Readings with the long-ITI session numbering, under the trial rule, give p 0.113 to 0.133. Per mouse, the OLS slope is negative in 14 of 18. The paper's r and p cannot both be matched under any reading. The first-listed reading measures the ITI from reward, the reading fig4b adopts.
deviations: The mixed model is fitted with statsmodels MixedLM (REML), random intercepts and slopes per mouse, in place of the Julia package the paper used. It is fitted with L-BFGS, Powell and Nelder-Mead and the converged fit with the highest REML likelihood is kept, as L-BFGS alone stopped at a lower optimum in some runs (fit, cue, samples, all sessions gave p = 0.014 in the round 2 notebook, against 0.00064 at the higher optimum).

outcomes.statement: Anticipatory lick rate increases across training sessions, in parallel with the deepening tonic dip (r = 0.65).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on tonic dopamine (Fig. 4C); Figure 4C legend
outcomes.quote: while anticipatory vigour increased in parallel (Fig. 4C, r = 0.65, p=so this 1e-4)

statistics.test: linear mixed-effects model with random intercepts and slopes per subject

outcomes.notes: Long-ITI sessions (reading a), session number among all sessions - fixed slope 0.103 Hz per session, p = 1.2e-05, pooled r 0.648 and within-mouse r 0.646, both within tolerance; with the long-ITI numbering slope 0.153, p = 1.9e-05, r 0.646. Over all sessions (reading b) slope 0.086, p = 8.7e-05, r 0.536, out of tolerance. Per mouse the long-ITI slope is positive in 15 of 18.

outcomes.statement: The approach-epoch selection of the Krausz hex-level data keeps 264,042 of 298,918 observations across 10 rats.
outcomes.source: Methods, Krausz (2023) dataset, paragraph 1; Methods, Datasets, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: This yielded 264,042 included observations across 10 rats
outcomes.notes: Dropping rows at a port (port not -100), rows with no distance to the chosen port (the start hex of each trial), rows at distance 0 and rows without velocity keeps 264,042 rows over 10 rats, the paper's count exactly. No row follows a reward within its trial, so "had already received reward" removes nothing.
deviations: The Methods do not name the columns; the mapping above is this attempt's, as the criterion asks.

outcomes.statement: In freely moving rats, NAc dopamine ramps up as the rats approach a reward port.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph after Figure 1 legend; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: DA ramped as animals approached their goals (Fig. 2A)
outcomes.notes: Per rat r between distance to the chosen port and mean DA at each distance is negative in 9 of 10 rats (mean -0.68, one-sample t(9) = -7.25, p = 4.8e-05). Averaging per hex position, as the Methods and the criterion say, with each hex at its mean distance, the mean r is -0.30, t(9) = -5.19, p = 0.00057, negative in 9 of 10. Across-rat mean DA is 0.18 at 1 hex and -0.13 at 20 hexes.
deviations: The criterion's "position-mean DA" is read two ways, the mean DA at each distance to the goal (the axis the paper plots; a hex position has many distances, as the goal changes by trial), and the mean DA at each hex position placed at its mean distance. Both are shown.

outcomes.statement: The dopamine ramp is steeper on approaches to high reward (80 µL or more) than to low reward (20 µL or less).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph after Figure 1 legend; Figure 2B legend
outcomes.quote: The ramp is steeper on approaches ending at high reward (>80 µL juice) versus low reward (< 20 µL)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), slope of DA on distance, high -0.0355 against low -0.0152 per hex, paired t(9) = -7.30, p = 4.6e-05; reading (b), mean DA, 0.120 against -0.002, t(9) = 7.75, p = 2.8e-05. Destination reward is the nominal reward of the port the trial ends at. Its values (10, 20, 50, 80, 90) are reward probabilities in percent in the Krausz et al. code, not µL as the paper says; the split at 80 and 20 is the same either way.

outcomes.statement: Ramps in early and late sessions look similar, with at most a modest reduction in ramp amplitude from early to late sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph after Figure 1 legend; Figure 2C legend
outcomes.quote: the ramps in early and late sessions look similar (i.e. the ramps do not flatten across time in the absence of learning)
outcomes.notes: Slope of DA on distance, early -0.0253 and late -0.0277 per hex (change -0.0024), paired t(9) = 0.67, p = 0.52, so the test does not find a difference. The ramp is slightly steeper late, not reduced as the Figure 2C legend says.
deviations: With 5 to 12 sessions per rat, a quartile is round(n/4) sessions, at least one (1 to 3); the Methods say only "first quartile" and "last quartile".

outcomes.statement: On fast approaches, dopamine is larger at the same positions than on slow ones.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph after Figure 1 legend; Figure 2D legend
outcomes.quote: fast trials show larger DA at the same positions, consistent with velocity scaling the ramp
outcomes.notes: At the 45 or 46 hex positions present in both velocity quartiles, mean DA is 0.162 on fast and -0.053 on slow observations, larger when fast in 10 of 10 rats, paired t(9) = 7.40, p = 4.1e-05.

outcomes.statement: Velocity co-varies with distance to goal, and average dopamine and velocity covary across distance.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph after Figure 1 legend; Figure 2E legend
outcomes.quote: We found that the velocity co-varied with the distance to goal (Fig. 2E)
outcomes.notes: Per rat r between distance and mean velocity, mean -0.66 (velocity higher nearer the goal), t(9) = -7.21, p = 5.0e-05; per rat r between mean DA and mean velocity across distance, mean 0.59, t(9) = 9.21, p = 7.1e-06.

outcomes.statement: The within-position coupling of velocity and dopamine increases with proximity to the goal (r = -0.494, df = 18, p = 0.027).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph after Figure 1 legend; Figure 2F
outcomes.quote: the velocity-dopamine coupling increased with proximity to goal, consistent with the idea that velocity scales with the gradient (Fig 2F, r=-0.494, df=18, p = 0.027)

statistics.test: correlation of within-position DA-velocity r with distance to goal

outcomes.notes: Reading (a), pooled within-distance DA-velocity r at distances 1 to 20, correlated with distance - r = -0.494, df = 18, p = 0.027, the paper's three values. Reading (b), per-rat r averaged, r = -0.579, p = 0.0075; reading (c), the 20 hex positions with most rows, r = 0.474, p = 0.035. Reading (a) over the 20 distances with the most rows (1 to 19 and 21) gives r = -0.560, p = 0.010, out of tolerance, so the match rests on taking the 20 distances nearest the goal.
deviations: The 20 distances of readings (a) and (b) are 1 to 20, the 20 nearest the goal; distance 21 has more rows than 20 (1097 against 908), and the 20 with the most rows are shown as well. The paper says only df = 18.

outcomes.statement: When rats are stationary (velocity below 5 cm/s), dopamine dips below zero (t = -4.27, df = 9, p = 0.001, one-tailed).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on the stationary prediction; Figure 2G-H legend
outcomes.quote: found that indeed the dopamine dipped below baseline (df =9, t = -4.27, p = 0.001, one-tailed) in instances where the rats’ velocity was near zero (Fig 2G-H)

statistics.test: one-sample t-test against zero across rats, one-tailed

outcomes.notes: Reading (b), all rows off the ports (approach rows and the start hex of each trial), stationary DA below zero in 9 of 10 rats, t(9) = -4.274, one-tailed p = 0.0010, the paper's values. Reading (a), approach rows only, t(9) = -2.81, p = 0.010, out of tolerance; with the rows at the ports added, t(9) = -1.46, p = 0.089. Moving against stationary, paired t(9) = 3.13 (p = 0.012) under (a) and 3.55 (p = 0.0062) under (b). Open for the authors - which rows the legend's "non-approach" observations are; the table has three kinds outside the approach selection (start hex, at a port, missing velocity), and only the reading without the port rows gives the reported t.
deviations: Assumed that "approach and non-approach" observations are all rows off the ports. The Figure 2G-H legend says both were used; the port rows are the rat at the port itself, before or after reward, which the Methods' selection also sets apart. All three row sets are shown.

outcomes.statement: The value function recovered from moving minus stationary dopamine shows a net increase toward the goal in 8 of 10 rats.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on internal consistency (Fig. 3A-B); Figure 3 legend
outcomes.quote: The recovered value function showed a net increase toward the goal in 8 out of 10 rats (A>0 in BIC winning model)
outcomes.notes: With no minimum number of observations per moving and stationary mean, the BIC-winning profile has A > 0 in 7 of 10 rats (the paper 8), and the recovered V is higher nearest the goal than farthest in 7 of 10. With at least 5 observations per mean, A > 0 in 6 of 10 (not reproduced under that reading). With the moving and stationary means taken from all rows off the ports (b1), the row set that matched Figure 2G-H, A > 0 in 7 and 6 of 10, the same counts. The approach rows are recorded, as the Methods name them, though fig2gh adopts (b1) for the same moving and stationary split; both row sets give 7. With the first round's narrower bounds of the profile scale the counts and winners are the same under all four readings. 5 of the 10 winning fits (no minimum, approach rows) run to the upper σ bound of 10,000 hexes, where the Gaussian is nearly quadratic in distance and the sign of A still gives the direction of the fitted change; the Gaussian wins there partly as a quadratic against nearly linear shapes. Under the minimum of 5, IM-1292 has A = -2.6e11 at σ = 0.78 (approach rows) and -5.2e10 at σ = 0.80 (b1; -2.44e12 in the round 2 notebook, as A is not determined for a Gaussian this narrow), a Gaussian that fits only the nearest point, which lies below the rest, and IM-1532's winning power law (approach rows) sits at the lower bound k = 1e-6 with A = 2.1e4. Open for the authors - the minimum count per position, which rows give the stationary means, how hex-position gradients are placed on the approach axis, and the forms of the four profiles.
deviations: The gradient is computed per hex position and distance to the goal, averaged per distance, and integrated toward the goal with scipy's RK45 (Dormand-Prince) on the linear interpolant, in place of Julia's Tsit5; both are explicit 5(4) Runge-Kutta solvers.

Profile forms as the criterion reads them (A exp(-λd) + c, A / (1 + kd) + c, A (d + 1)^(-k) + c, A exp(-d²/2σ²) + c); BIC = n ln(SSE/n) + k ln n. A and c are solved by least squares for each value of the shape parameter, which is searched on a grid and refined. The shape parameter is kept positive (a profile decaying with distance), as the paper reads A > 0 as a net increase toward the goal, which holds only for a decaying profile; it is searched from 1e-6 to 20 per hex (hyperbolic to 1000) and σ from 0.1 to 10,000 hexes.
In the (b1) row set the start hex of each trial, which has no distance in the table, is placed one hex beyond the trial's next row; the approach rows (a) are the reading recorded.
Assumed no minimum observation count, the literal reading of the Methods, which name none; the minimum of 5 is shown as the other reading.

outcomes.statement: All four candidate shapes fit each rat's recovered value function well (mean R² above 0.8), and the best shape varies across rats, Gaussian in 8, exponential in 1 and power-law in 1.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on internal consistency (Fig. 3C-D); Figure 3 legend
outcomes.quote: All four provided good fits (mean R² > 0.8), with the best-fitting shape varying across rats ... a Gaussian profile won in 8, exponential in 1, and power-law in 1 (Fig 3C-D)
outcomes.notes: The Gaussian profile wins in 9 of 10 rats under both readings; the tenth is exponential with no minimum count and power-law with a minimum of 5 (the paper 8, 1, 1). Mean R² over rats is 0.54 to 0.73 for the four shapes with no minimum, and 0.77 to 0.82 with a minimum of 5, where three of four exceed 0.8. With all rows off the ports (b1) the Gaussian wins in 10 of 10 with no minimum and in 8 of 10, with 1 exponential and 1 hyperbolic, with a minimum of 5; mean R² 0.50 to 0.68 and 0.77 to 0.81, two of four above 0.8. Measured values are from the approach rows with no minimum.
deviations: Fits and readings as in fig3-recovered-value-increases.

outcomes.statement: Of six models of approach dopamine, the Gaussian continuous-time TD model fits best summed across rats and wins in 8 of 10 rats by BIC.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on model comparison (Fig. 5B-C); Figure 5B-C legend
outcomes.quote: The Gaussian CT TD model provided the best fit across rats (Fig. 5B, Krausz 2023 dataset), and was also winning in 8 of 10 individual rats by BIC (Fig. 5C)
outcomes.notes: Summed over rats, Gaussian CT TD has the lowest BIC; the others are higher by 412 (CT TD exponential), 948 (dV/dt Gaussian), 1623 (Value), 1866 (dV/dt exponential) and 6628 (Velocity). Gaussian CT TD wins in 8 of 10 rats, dV/dt Gaussian in 2. With λ free to go below zero, the CT TD exponential and Value fits of IM-1322, IM-1398 and IM-1532 take a negative λ (a profile rising with distance) and lower their SSE by 0.53 to 20.93; with the first round's search (λ from 1e-4 to 5, σ from 0.3 to 100) CT TD exponential was 473 higher and Value 1679, with the same winners. One fit (IM-1322, Gaussian CT TD) runs to the upper σ bound (9998 hexes), its SSE (11621.02) 0.17 below the fit at σ = 100. A Nelder-Mead search over all parameters from each optimum lowers no SSE by more than 1e-7.
deviations: The Methods fit all parameters by multi-start Nelder-Mead (4 initial vectors and 10 perturbations each). Here the linear parameters are solved by least squares for each value of the spatial scale, which is searched on a grid (λ from -5 to 5 per hex, 301 values; σ from 0.3 to 10,000 hexes, 200 values) and refined, then checked by Nelder-Mead from the optimum. This finds the least-squares optimum without random starts.

outcomes.statement: In a factorial decomposition, the tonic term improves fit by ΔBIC = 1156 and the Gaussian spatial profile by ΔBIC = 706.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on model comparison (Fig. 5D); Figure 5D legend
outcomes.quote: The tonic term −ρV̂ improved fit by ΔBIC =1156, while the Gaussian ... profile improved fit by ΔBIC = 706
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), main effects over the 2 x 2 design - tonic term ΔBIC 1201.0 and Gaussian profile ΔBIC 665.0, both within tolerance (1040 to 1272 and 635 to 777). Reading (b) gives 948.2 and 412.2, reading (c) 1453.8 and 917.8, both out of tolerance. With the first round's narrower search of the spatial scale (λ not below 1e-4, σ up to 100) reading (a) gave 1170.1 and 695.6; allowing λ below zero moved both by 31.

outcomes.statement: In an independent dataset of mice running without a spatial goal, dopamine does not track velocity, as the model predicts when there is no spatial value gradient.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph before Table 1; Discussion, paragraph 10; Supplementary Figure S2 (not in the text read)
outcomes.quote: correctly predicts no dopamine-velocity coupling in the absence of a spatial value gradient (confirmed in an independent dataset of mice running without a spatial goal25, Supplementary Figure S2)
outcomes.notes: The analysis is in Supplementary Figure S2, which was not available; the main text gives no selection, measure or test, and a claim of absence is judged on the paper's own test. The paper does not say where the Brown et al. (2026) data are held, and the code on OSF (osf.io/g3e2d) is not public (its API answered 401 on 2026-11-25). DANDI:001552 holds no Brown et al. data (502 assets, all from the Floeder mice), and the bioRxiv supplementary page answered 429 on 2026-11-25.
outcomes.where: Brown et al. (2026), Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-025-10083-1; the repository holding its data is not named in the text read

findings.statement: Two recordings are deposited twice under different days. sub-JF-dLight-ramp2-F2 Day3 and Day4 hold identical photometry (381,921 samples), cues and licks, as do sub-JF-dLight-ramp2-F4 Day5 and Day6 (330,189 samples). An analysis that counts sessions counts each of them twice, and one of each pair is filed under a day on which, as far as the files show, no other recording exists.
findings.checked: Shown, and critical is right. Cell 9 shows identical 470 hashes, sample counts (381,921 and 330,189), cue counts and lick counts for F2 Day3/Day4 and F4 Day5/Day6. Cue and lick identity is shown only through the counts. One recording deposited as two, labelled as different days, is critical by definition.

findings.statement: The photometry and the event log are on different clocks and the files do not say so. Every photometry series states a start of 0 (at most 8 microseconds), while the event log has its own zero; aligned by the TTL2 channel, the photometry starts 3.6 to 251 s before the event log's zero. The only link is photometry_ttl2, described in every file only as "raw photometry channel ttl2", whose rising edges fall on the cue onsets (event code 15). A user who takes both time bases as given places dopamine seconds to minutes away from the cues and rewards.
findings.checked: Shown in substance, and critical is right. Cell 7 shows TTL2 edges fitting cue times within 0.094 s, and the photometry starting 3.6 to 251.3 s before the event-log zero. "Starts at time 0" and the TTL2 description are not printed. Signals on different clocks with no stated link are critical; the 64 files with the wrong rate would make the problem visible, but the other 292 sessions would not.

findings.statement: 64 of the 144 JF-FP photometry series state a rate of 120481.9 Hz, or timestamps 8.3 microseconds apart, for signals sampled at 120.3 to 120.5 Hz (fitted from TTL2 edges against cue times), a factor of about 1000. The other files state 130 Hz, which the TTL2 fit confirms.

The 144 files of the 9 JF-VR-FP mice (all opened) hold only raw photometry and TTL channels (session description "photometry_only") with no event log, task parameters, behaviour or processing module, and nothing in the dandiset says which experiment they belong to or how to align them to a task. They cannot be analysed as deposited.

The TTL channels, the eventFlag series (described only as the third column of the event log) and the meaning of the lick code in use (code 5, "Lick3 onset") are not explained, and the stretches where the 470 signal is near zero (about 2950 samples, some 23 s, in JF-dLight-ramp2-M4 Day9 and JF-dLight-ramp2-M5 Day9) are not marked as dropouts.

The sessions are in blocks of 8 long-ITI then 8 short-ITI sessions (JF-FP) or 7 or 8 long, 8 short, 7 or 8 long (JF-dLight-ramp2), with median inter-cue intervals of about 53.7 and 16.6 s, and rewards 9 s after each cue. Garud and Morris describe the sessions as alternating across days, with ITIs of ~8 and ~55 s (Results) or ~15 and ~45 s (Methods).

paper_notes.statement: The paper gives the Floeder ITIs as ~8 s and ~55 s in the Results and as ~15 s and ~45 s median in the Methods, and the Figure 2B reward split as > 80 and < 20 µL in the legend and ≥ 80 and ≤ 20 µL in the Methods.

Questions for the authors on Figure 4. How was the 405 nm signal regressed out and ΔF/F formed; is the ITI midpoint measured from reward or from the cue; is an "observation" in the 20-observation rule a trial or a sample; is session number counted over all sessions or long-ITI sessions only; and is the printed r a pooled Pearson r, a within-mouse r, or derived from the mixed model? Every combination was run; the slope is negative under all 16, but r = -0.29 with p < 0.001 is matched under none, and only the within-mouse r is near -0.29.

Questions for the authors on Figures 2G-H and 3. Which rows of hexLevelDf are the "non-approach" observations of Figure 2G-H (all rows off the ports reproduce t = -4.27 exactly; adding the rows at the ports does not)? For the value recovery, what minimum number of moving and stationary observations was required at a position, how were hex-position gradients ordered along the approach axis, and what are the four three-parameter profiles? With no minimum, 7 of 10 rats have A > 0 and the mean R² is below 0.8, with the approach rows and with all rows off the ports.

The supplement (cited for further detailed methods and for Supplementary Figure S2) was not available, and the code at osf.io/g3e2d is not public (the OSF API answers 401), so no method detail could be checked against the code.

The paper gives the Krausz et al. destination reward in µL (> 80 and < 20 µL juice in the Figure 2B legend, ≥ 80 and ≤ 20 µL in the Methods). The table's nom_rwd columns take the values 10, 20, 50, 80 and 90, and the Krausz et al. code (Berke-lab/DA_maze, DA/Modules/hexLevelAnalyses.py) divides them by 100 and calls them pRwd, so they are reward probabilities in percent. The split at 80 and 20 is the same under either reading.
